metadata.narrative: I'm currently working on a project. The professor wasn't clear, she just said that I will use NLP techniques on some data, de-identified Electronic Health Records, to extract Asian subgroups, and try to abstract the same subgroups as are in CDC WONDER data. Then, I'll apply this to look at prevalence rates of autoimmune diseases. I have no clue what she means. Can you first help explain what she might mean? I don't know examples of what Electronic Health Records look like. What NLP techniques might I be using on data like this? What subgroups in CDC WONDER data would I be abstracting? How could I apply this to look at prevalence rates of autoimmune diseases? What skills should I brush up on? Please help me create a plan for my research going forward, according to what the professor said.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and strict-JSON cited sentence answers.

answer.text: Your professor is describing a project with four linked steps: use NLP to pull demographic and clinical information out of de-identified EHR text, split aggregated 'Asian' patients into finer ethnic subgroups, match those subgroups to CDC WONDER's race/ethnicity categories, and compute/compare autoimmune-disease prevalence rates across subgroups.
EHR data comes in two flavors: 'fielded' structured data in defined database fields (e.g., a sex field limited to M/F/N) and free-text narrative such as a chief complaint that has no fixed format.

Real de-identified research EHR corpora you might practice on resemble MIMIC-III (over 40,000 ICU patients from Beth Israel Deaconess, 2001–2012) or the i2b2 datasets combining clinical and billing data.

A concrete example of NLP extraction is turning 'Levofloxacin 500 mg p.o. q.d. for a seven day course' into structured fields for drug, dosage, route, and frequency, or flagging 'chest pain' while using negation detection to know a symptom was denied rather than present.

Core clinical-NLP techniques include dictionary/rule-based lookup (MedLEE), full pipelines with sentence splitting, section detection, negation, and named-entity recognition (cTAKES, CogStack, CLAMP), and hybrid rule-plus-machine-learning systems.
Commercial APIs like Amazon Comprehend Medical extract entities such as conditions and medications and map them to standard vocabularies like SNOMED CT and RxNorm.

More advanced work benchmarks concept extraction on shared tasks like the 2010 i2b2/VA challenge and uses deep-learning 'computable phenotyping' to algorithmically define which patients count as disease cases from EHR text.

CDC WONDER's mortality databases generally break race into broad categories—American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian/Pacific Islander combined, Black, and White—plus a separate Hispanic-origin flag, so 'Asian' is not natively disaggregated there.
CDC WONDER's natality data similarly reports a single 'non-Hispanic Asian' category rather than splitting Asian into ethnic subgroups.
Your task is essentially to build finer subgroup labels from EHR text and see how they map onto (and reveal what is hidden by) WONDER's coarser categories.

One published method for extracting Asian subgroups combines a patient's EHR race, ethnicity, and language fields with a validated Asian-surname list to classify people into groups like South Asian, Chinese, and Other Asian.
A parallel survey-based approach splits Asian into Chinese, Asian Indian, and Other Asian using a self-reported ancestry question, useful if your EHR has a similar field.

When structured race/ethnicity fields are missing or too coarse, deep-learning imputation methods such as RIDDLE can predict race/ethnicity from a patient's diagnosis history, complementing surname- or census-based imputation.

An important caution is that machine-learning models can infer a patient's race from clinical notes even after explicit racial words are removed, so any extraction pipeline should be checked for encoded bias.

'De-identified' EHR data usually means the 18 HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers (names, most dates, contact info, medical record numbers, etc.) have been stripped, or an expert-certified 'Statistical/Expert Determination' method kept re-identification risk low while retaining some quasi-identifiers.

For the autoimmune-disease side, researchers build 'computable phenotype' algorithms combining ICD-9/10 codes, labs (e.g., a positive antinuclear antibody titer), and NLP-detected keywords (e.g., 'Raynaud's phenomenon') to flag likely cases, reporting positive predictive value and sensitivity against manual chart review.

Some phenotypes build a single 'umbrella' algorithm spanning many autoimmune diseases, typically requiring a diagnosis code on at least three separate days spanning at least a week before counting someone as a case.

Broader EHR phenotyping frameworks, such as eMERGE, explicitly list race and ethnicity as core demographic variables alongside ICD codes, labs, and medications, and distinguish structured data from unstructured notes requiring NLP.

Once you have subgroup labels and disease cases, disaggregating 'Asian' reveals real differences: a UK EHR chart review of systemic lupus erythematosus found distinct clinical and autoantibody profiles in Bangladeshi patients versus other ethnic groups.

Population-level SLE prevalence estimates differ sharply by Asian subgroup: about 46 per 100,000 in Malaysian Chinese versus 26 in Indians and 12 in Malays, and 33 versus 10 per 100,000 in Hawaii's Chinese versus Europeans, showing why lumping all Asians together obscures disease burden.

This mirrors non-autoimmune findings: California Health Interview Survey data show Filipino adults with the most disparities after disaggregation while Chinese appear healthiest, and Kaiser Permanente EHR data show diabetes prevalence ranging from 15.6% in Chinese to 31.9% in Filipino patients, patterns invisible in an aggregated 'Asian' category.

To make valid prevalence comparisons across subgroups and against national figures, you need both crude prevalence and age-adjusted prevalence using direct standardization to a reference population such as the 2000 US Census age distribution.

Skills worth brushing up on include Python and regular expressions for text pattern-matching, familiarity with medical coding/terminology systems (ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, UMLS), and basic NLP/machine-learning concepts.
Also refresh biostatistics for rate calculation and get hands-on practice with a clinical NLP toolkit (cTAKES, CLAMP, or similar) on a sample corpus before touching real de-identified data.

Plan step 1: confirm with your professor which EHR source, which race/ethnicity or surname fields exist, and which autoimmune disease(s) are targeted, since this determines whether you need surname-based, self-report-based, or imputation-based subgroup extraction.
Step 2: explore the EHR's structured fields versus free-text notes and practice your pipeline on an open corpus like MIMIC-III or i2b2 before running it on real data.

Step 3: build or adapt an NLP pipeline (rule-based lexicon plus machine-learning NER, using cTAKES/CLAMP or a commercial API) to extract race, ethnicity, and disease mentions, auditing it for racial-inference bias.

Step 4: define Asian subgroup categories using validated approaches and map them onto CDC WONDER's coarser 'Asian/Pacific Islander' or 'non-Hispanic Asian' categories to show what disaggregation adds.

Step 5: build and validate a computable phenotype for your target autoimmune disease(s) using ICD codes, labs, and NLP keywords, checking positive predictive value against a manually chart-reviewed sample.

Step 6: calculate crude and age-adjusted prevalence rates per Asian subgroup, compare them to the aggregated-Asian rate and national CDC WONDER estimates, and interpret differences against prior disaggregation findings.
Finally, document de-identification constraints and any bias risks in your NLP-derived race/ethnicity labels as explicit limitations when presenting results.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counterevidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counterevidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

First satisfy the concrete minimum requirements. If budget remains, improve
toward the target/excellence requirements by strengthening thin coverage,
checking important claims, resolving contradictions, and adding materially
useful evidence.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and respond with only one JSON
object, with no prose or Markdown fences, exactly shaped as:

`{"answer": [{"text": "<one sentence>", "citations": ["<docid>", "..."]}]}`

- Each answer item is one sentence in reading order.
- Each `citations` array contains zero to three committed docids that directly
  support that sentence.
- Every factual sentence should be supported.
- Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- The complete report must contain at most 1024 words.
- If validation feedback identifies invalid JSON, uncommitted citations,
  excessive citations, or excessive length, correct the response on the next
  turn in this same continuous conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

answer.text: Your professor is describing a project with four linked steps: use NLP to pull demographic and clinical information out of de-identified EHR text, split aggregated 'Asian' patients into finer ethnic subgroups, match those subgroups to CDC WONDER's race/ethnicity categories, and compute/compare autoimmune-disease prevalence rates across subgroups.
EHR data comes in two flavors: 'fielded' structured data in defined database fields (e.g., a sex field limited to M/F/N) and free-text narrative such as a chief complaint that has no fixed format.

Real de-identified research EHR corpora you might practice on resemble MIMIC-III (over 40,000 ICU patients from Beth Israel Deaconess, 2001–2012) or the i2b2 datasets combining clinical and billing data.

A concrete example of NLP extraction is turning 'Levofloxacin 500 mg p.o. q.d. for a seven day course' into structured fields for drug, dosage, route, and frequency, or flagging 'chest pain' while using negation detection to know a symptom was denied rather than present.

Core clinical-NLP techniques include dictionary/rule-based lookup (MedLEE), full pipelines with sentence splitting, section detection, negation, and named-entity recognition (cTAKES, CogStack, CLAMP), and hybrid rule-plus-machine-learning systems.
Commercial APIs like Amazon Comprehend Medical extract entities such as conditions and medications and map them to standard vocabularies like SNOMED CT and RxNorm.

More advanced work benchmarks concept extraction on shared tasks like the 2010 i2b2/VA challenge and uses deep-learning 'computable phenotyping' to algorithmically define which patients count as disease cases from EHR text.

CDC WONDER's mortality databases generally break race into broad categories—American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian/Pacific Islander combined, Black, and White—plus a separate Hispanic-origin flag, so 'Asian' is not natively disaggregated there.
CDC WONDER's natality data similarly reports a single 'non-Hispanic Asian' category rather than splitting Asian into ethnic subgroups.
Your task is essentially to build finer subgroup labels from EHR text and see how they map onto (and reveal what is hidden by) WONDER's coarser categories.

One published method for extracting Asian subgroups combines a patient's EHR race, ethnicity, and language fields with a validated Asian-surname list to classify people into groups like South Asian, Chinese, and Other Asian.
A parallel survey-based approach splits Asian into Chinese, Asian Indian, and Other Asian using a self-reported ancestry question, useful if your EHR has a similar field.

When structured race/ethnicity fields are missing or too coarse, deep-learning imputation methods such as RIDDLE can predict race/ethnicity from a patient's diagnosis history, complementing surname- or census-based imputation.

An important caution is that machine-learning models can infer a patient's race from clinical notes even after explicit racial words are removed, so any extraction pipeline should be checked for encoded bias.

'De-identified' EHR data usually means the 18 HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers (names, most dates, contact info, medical record numbers, etc.) have been stripped, or an expert-certified 'Statistical/Expert Determination' method kept re-identification risk low while retaining some quasi-identifiers.

For the autoimmune-disease side, researchers build 'computable phenotype' algorithms combining ICD-9/10 codes, labs (e.g., a positive antinuclear antibody titer), and NLP-detected keywords (e.g., 'Raynaud's phenomenon') to flag likely cases, reporting positive predictive value and sensitivity against manual chart review.

Some phenotypes build a single 'umbrella' algorithm spanning many autoimmune diseases, typically requiring a diagnosis code on at least three separate days spanning at least a week before counting someone as a case.

Broader EHR phenotyping frameworks, such as eMERGE, explicitly list race and ethnicity as core demographic variables alongside ICD codes, labs, and medications, and distinguish structured data from unstructured notes requiring NLP.

Once you have subgroup labels and disease cases, disaggregating 'Asian' reveals real differences: a UK EHR chart review of systemic lupus erythematosus found distinct clinical and autoantibody profiles in Bangladeshi patients versus other ethnic groups.

Population-level SLE prevalence estimates differ sharply by Asian subgroup: about 46 per 100,000 in Malaysian Chinese versus 26 in Indians and 12 in Malays, and 33 versus 10 per 100,000 in Hawaii's Chinese versus Europeans, showing why lumping all Asians together obscures disease burden.

This mirrors non-autoimmune findings: California Health Interview Survey data show Filipino adults with the most disparities after disaggregation while Chinese appear healthiest, and Kaiser Permanente EHR data show diabetes prevalence ranging from 15.6% in Chinese to 31.9% in Filipino patients, patterns invisible in an aggregated 'Asian' category.

To make valid prevalence comparisons across subgroups and against national figures, you need both crude prevalence and age-adjusted prevalence using direct standardization to a reference population such as the 2000 US Census age distribution.

Skills worth brushing up on include Python and regular expressions for text pattern-matching, familiarity with medical coding/terminology systems (ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, UMLS), and basic NLP/machine-learning concepts.
Also refresh biostatistics for rate calculation and get hands-on practice with a clinical NLP toolkit (cTAKES, CLAMP, or similar) on a sample corpus before touching real de-identified data.

Plan step 1: confirm with your professor which EHR source, which race/ethnicity or surname fields exist, and which autoimmune disease(s) are targeted, since this determines whether you need surname-based, self-report-based, or imputation-based subgroup extraction.
Step 2: explore the EHR's structured fields versus free-text notes and practice your pipeline on an open corpus like MIMIC-III or i2b2 before running it on real data.

Step 3: build or adapt an NLP pipeline (rule-based lexicon plus machine-learning NER, using cTAKES/CLAMP or a commercial API) to extract race, ethnicity, and disease mentions, auditing it for racial-inference bias.

Step 4: define Asian subgroup categories using validated approaches and map them onto CDC WONDER's coarser 'Asian/Pacific Islander' or 'non-Hispanic Asian' categories to show what disaggregation adds.

Step 5: build and validate a computable phenotype for your target autoimmune disease(s) using ICD codes, labs, and NLP keywords, checking positive predictive value against a manually chart-reviewed sample.

Step 6: calculate crude and age-adjusted prevalence rates per Asian subgroup, compare them to the aggregated-Asian rate and national CDC WONDER estimates, and interpret differences against prior disaggregation findings.
Finally, document de-identification constraints and any bias risks in your NLP-derived race/ethnicity labels as explicit limitations when presenting results.
